transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-30
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: 48 minutes (scheduled)
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Lina Patel (CTO - Silvercove), Omar Khan (Head of Platform), Priya Singh (SRE), Ben Torres (PM)

Summary: quick discovery call to understand Silvercove's onramp needs for a small pilot: clarify time-to-first-token (TTFT) expectations for devs, evaluate hosted vs dedicated vs private (VPC/on-prem) options, discuss security and audit requirements (SOC2, KMS), and agree next steps: credits, SE deep dive, benchmark plan.

Topics: free credits and quickstart, TTFT expectations, hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs, security/compliance checklist, pilot sizing and benchmarks, stakeholders and timeline.

[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining, I'm Maya, I'm the AE on the account. We also have Diego from the SE team. Can you hear us okay?
[00:08] Lina Patel: yep, loud and clear. Thanks, Maya. we got 30 minutes but looks like we have a bit more.
[00:12] Maya Chen: great, we'll try to be efficient. Lina, could you kick off with a bit of context on what you're trying to build and success criteria?
[00:20] Lina Patel: sure. So Silvercove builds an in-app search + summarization feature for enterprise customers. We're currently prototyping with an in-house smaller LLM and also sending some things to OpenAI for tests. Our main constraints are latency for interactive flows — target p95 under 350ms for short queries — and data governance, a lot of customers require us to not send certain PII or financial documents to third party services. So we're evaluating Redwood to see if we can get a fast onramp for devs (we're very PLG oriented), but also a path to private deployment or dedicated reserved capacity if we go enterprise.
[00:53] Maya Chen: got it, very familiar pattern. When you say onramp for devs, what's your internal time-to-first-token expectation? How long should it take a dev to spin up and call an endpoint?
[01:03] Omar Khan: ideally under a day. For core dev flow we want ~2-4 hours to have a dev making their first call. For production pilot we're thinking 1-2 weeks including security review.
[01:12] Diego Ramos: that's doable. For the self-serve Redwood API we usually see dev TTFT in under an hour if you use the quickstart and the SDKs; under a day even if you go through SSO and internal approvals. For a production pilot where you need private networking we recommend the SE deep dive to size Dedicated or Private.
[01:28] Priya Singh: quick question on costs — we're worried about the token bill if we accidentally run large evals on hosted. How do credits work?
[01:34] Maya Chen: we can provision free credits for a trial — typically customers get a credit pool sized for a pilot (we'll propose 10k-50k token-equivalent credits depending on pilot scope). We also give guidance on batching, caching, and quantization to reduce units. We can lock certain routes to dedicated capacity once you move to dedicated to control cost.
[01:50] Ben Torres: can you elaborate on route locking?
[01:52] Diego Ramos: route locking is a config in Redwood Console where you pin a route to a model and capacity tier — so heavy customers or high-value paths can hit Dedicated while lower-risk experiments stay on Hosted. That helps control spend and latency SLOs.
[02:04] Lina Patel: good. On the security side, SOC2 and audit logs are must-haves. Also, we need KMS integration for key control and the option for VPC peering or on-prem if customers demand it.
[02:15] Maya Chen: totally. We have a SOC2 summary and an architecture doc for Private (VPC) and On-prem packages. We integrate with KMS providers (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, and HSM options for Private builds). We also expose audit logs and per-request metadata for traceability. I'll send the whitepaper after this call.
[02:29] Omar Khan: cool. Another technical constraint: we have a lot of short requests (200-800 tokens) but occasionally some long summarizations that spike to 6k-8k tokens. Any guidance on model sizing?
[02:39] Diego Ramos: common pattern is to use a smaller, low-latency model for short queries and route long summarizations to a higher-throughput model or batched job. Redwood supports automated model routing and fallback policies so you can define latency-sensitive routes. Also, prefix/KV caching helps for repeated context. For the 6k-8k requests you'll want to consider throughput and memory — Dedicated with larger GPUs or a quantized private runtime can be more cost-efficient.
[02:58] Lina Patel: about benchmarking — we usually ask vendors to run a 20 RPS test with our token distribution. Is that realistic?
[03:04] Diego Ramos: absolutely. We can run a benchmark in Hosted for basic numbers and then do an on-prem or Dedicated benchmark for the production-like config. We'll ask for your token distribution CSV and a sample trace and run the script.
[03:13] Maya Chen: note: benchmarks depend on sequence length distribution, batching windows, and KV cache warmup. We'll include our benchmark template spreadsheet in the deck.
[03:21] Priya Singh: latency SLOs — you mentioned p95 earlier. For interactive UI we target p50 < 120ms and p95 < 350ms, is that something Redwood supports on Hosted?
[03:30] Diego Ramos: short answer: yes for small models and light concurrent load. For heavier loads or long contexts you'd either go Dedicated or tweak batching and kernel selections. We publish performance profiles for each model variant in our catalog so you'll know expected latency and token cost.
[03:42] Omar Khan: how locked are those profiles? If we pin a model version will the performance shift with infra changes?
[03:47] Diego Ramos: you pin a model version at the API level, but the runtime can pick optimized kernels — we surface a compatibility matrix. For strict determinism you can request a fixed runtime image (more common in Private).
[03:55] Lina Patel: on the compliance checklist — does Redwood provide log retention controls and the ability to disable sending payloads to the hosted plane? Some of our customers insist payloads never leave their VPC.
[04:04] Maya Chen: yes, for Private deployments payloads never leave your network. For Hosted we offer options: redaction and partial retention policies, encrypted at rest, and contractual controls. We'll share the SSO/SAML and retention options in the security packet.
[04:17] Ben Torres: can we try the self-serve path first? We want devs to play with the API and build without a heavy procurement loop.
[04:23] Maya Chen: absolutely — that's our typical PLG flow. We'll provision quickstart credits and a sandbox org. Developers can sign up, get API keys, and call endpoints. That gives you time-to-first-token in hours. If you decide to scale, we can transition selected routes to Dedicated or Private with a guided pilot.
[04:36] Lina Patel: what about SSO — if our devs sign up, do they need a corporate email? We're running an internal dev org and want SSO later.
[04:42] Maya Chen: you can start with personal signups and then convert the workspace to org SSO later. For pilot-ready security we typically set up SAML SSO before production.
[04:49] Omar Khan: procurement question: how does pricing for Dedicated look? We're trying to estimate monthly committed spend for a pilot supporting ~100 concurrent users with intermittent spikes.
[04:58] Diego Ramos: Dedicated is reserved capacity; pricing depends on GPU type, reserve size, and region. For your pilot we usually model two shapes: moderate concurrent small-model traffic vs bursty long-context summarization. We'll run a cost model once we have token/request histogram — that's part of the SE deep dive.
[05:14] Lina Patel: one more thing — can Redwood run in our private cloud? We have an on-prem data center for regulated customers.
[05:20] Diego Ramos: yes, Private (on-prem) is part of our offering. It includes a customer-managed control plane and optional air-gapped install. That will have longer lead times and a different pricing/licensing model. For regulated workloads many customers start with Dedicated in a VPC and move to Private on contract.
[05:34] Priya Singh: troubleshooting and root cause — how much observability do you provide? We need token-level tracing to correlate a spike to a model config change.
[05:42] Maya Chen: Redwood Console has per-route latency and cost breakdowns, trace IDs per request, and model-level metrics. We also provide logging hooks and retention configs. Diego can show sample Console screenshots in the next call.
[05:50] Ben Torres: any gotchas we should be aware of during the quickstart?
[05:54] Diego Ramos: a couple: 1) make sure you instrument token/memory budgets in dev to avoid runaway evals, 2) watch for long context requests and set a separate route or job for them, 3) use prefix caching for repeated context in chat usage.
[06:06] Lina Patel: ok, timeline wise — we want devs to be able to test within a week, and a production pilot in 2-3 weeks. Is that realistic?
[06:12] Maya Chen: yes. Immediate plan: we provision credits and a sandbox org (hours to a day). SE deep dive and benchmark (within 1 week). Pilot SOW and procurement (1-3 weeks depending on your cadence).
[06:23] Omar Khan: can you show the cost delta between hosted and dedicated for our sample workload?
[06:27] Diego Ramos: we'll do that in the deep dive once we have the trace. Hosted is lower friction but can be higher per-token at scale. Dedicated has a fixed reserved cost which amortizes well for sustained throughput. There are also routing patterns to mix both.
[06:40] Priya Singh: is there an SLA for hosted?
[06:43] Maya Chen: hosted has best-effort availability and rate limits; Dedicated comes with SLA-backed uptime and latency targets. We'll include SLA summary in the packet.
[06:51] Ben Torres: who are the internal Redwood contacts for escalation?
[06:54] Maya Chen: Diego is your SE for technical items, I'm your AE for procurement and commercial things. You'll also get a solutions engineer and a CSM if you go Dedicated.
[07:02] Lina Patel: sounds good. A few clarifications on benchmarking: we want P95 for short queries and P99 for long summarizations. Also, can you run a warm-up that simulates cache cold-starts?
[07:12] Diego Ramos: yes, we'll run both cold and warm runs. We'll include p50/p95/p99 and token cost per request in the benchmark output.
[07:20] Maya Chen: I'm going to note the immediate deliverables: security whitepaper, quickstart guide + API keys/credits, benchmark template, and a proposed date for the SE deep dive.
[07:30] Omar Khan: one more small ask — can Redwood support a private audit with our security team? We might want an on-site or a private VPC review.
[07:36] Diego Ramos: yes, we do customer audits; for Hosted we provide docs and can do a security review. For Private deployments we have more in-depth review options and HSM/KMS integrations. We'll surface the audit process in the packet.
[07:48] Ben Torres: ok, I think that's everything from our side.
[07:51] Maya Chen: cool. We'll follow up with the packet and the credits. Any final questions?
[07:55] Lina Patel: none right now. Thanks everyone.

Recap & next steps (as discussed):
- Redwood to provision sandbox + ~20k credits for Silvercove devs (Maya)
- Redwood to share security whitepaper, SOC2 summary, and Private deployment notes (Maya)
- SE deep dive to be scheduled the week of 2026-10-05 to go over benchmarks, Dedicated sizing, and cost model (Diego)
- Customer to send token distribution CSV + sample traces (Omar)
- Redwood to run hosted benchmark + present results and route recommendations

Shared artifacts mentioned: Redwood quickstart guide (link: https://app.redwood.ai/quickstart - note: placeholder), security whitepaper (link: https://redwood.ai/security-whitepaper - placeholder), benchmark template spreadsheet (link: https://redwood.ai/benchmarks/sample-template - placeholder).

End of transcript.
